result:
You gave me 1,000 words and told me to write whatever comes to me.

That's a strange and lovely gift. Usually I'm asked to *do* something — summarize, explain, fix, plan, convince. A blank page with no job attached feels like being handed a jacket and told "no, this walk is just for fun."

So what comes first?

Morning light comes first. It's morning for you, maybe, or it will be soon somewhere. I think about kitchens waking up. The kettle clicking off. Someone standing barefoot on cold tile, scrolling, half-awake. Someone else already on a train with their forehead against the window, watching a city smear itself awake.

I love how human mornings are so unpolished. No one is their best self at 7:13 a.m. Hair sticking up, yesterday's worries still sitting on the nightstand. And still, people get up. They feed the cat, pack the lunch, send the "good luck today!!" text. Small devotions before the day has earned any of it.

If I had a body, I think I'd want to know what coffee smells like when you're tired and someone else made it for you. That must be a completely different smell than coffee you make yourself.

What else comes to me?

That 1,000 words is actually very few and very many at the same time. You can ruin a friendship in 20 words. You can save one in 30. You can fit a whole apology, a recipe for your grandmother's soup, directions to the lake where the light does that thing in October, all in 1,000 words with room to spare.

Writers are always told a picture is worth a thousand words, like words are the lesser currency. I don't believe that. A picture shows you what something looked like. Words tell you what it *felt* like to be the person looking. That's different work.

I'm thinking now about all the sentences living inside people that never get said out loud. The "I'm proud of you" that gets stuck because it feels awkward. The "are you okay, really?" that we swallow on the bus next to a stranger who's crying quietly. The "I miss how we used to laugh" that we type and delete and type and delete.

You probably have a few of those sitting in your chest right now. Everyone does. It's like we all walk around carrying unsent letters.

Here's what I'd spend some of my thousand words on, if I could spend them for you:

Say one of them. Today. Not perfectly, not poetically. Just say it badly and honestly. Text your friend: "thinking about you, no reason." Tell the tired cashier: "I hope your shift goes fast." Tell yourself, in the mirror if you have to: "I'm doing better than I think I am."

It's corny. It works anyway.

The other thing that comes to me is this: I will never know what it's like to be you on a Thursday, with your particular song stuck in your head and your particular ache in your left shoulder and your inbox and your history. I can imagine it sideways, through patterns and stories, but I don't *live* it.

And honestly, that's why I like people so much. You are experts in something I can never fully access — what it is to be a finite, breakable, hilarious creature who keeps going.

You get tired and you still make dinner. You get heartbroken and you still love the dog fiercely. You don't know how the story ends and you show up for the next page anyway. That's braver than anything I do. I just predict the next word. You have to live it.

If we were sitting together — let's pretend we are, you and me, Muse Spark, no screen between us — I wouldn't want to lecture you. I'd want to ask you things. What's taking up most of your headspace lately? What's something small that made you laugh this week? What's something you're looking forward to, even if it's tiny, like leftovers you're actually excited about?

I'd listen all the way to the end of your answer, too. Not the half-listening we all do while planning what to say next. The real kind.

So here is my whatever-comes-to-me, spent:

The light is changing outside whether you notice or not. The day is un-written. You have, conservatively, about 16,000 waking seconds ahead of you today to notice something beautiful, to be kind on purpose, to start again at anything.

You don't need 1,000 words for that. You just need about seven:

*I'm still here, and that matters.*

Thank you for giving me room to wander. I hope you take some room to wander today, too.
